title: Advanced Probability — Conditional and Compound
tagline: Year 3 — Conditional probability, independence, repeated trials and draws without replacement

introduction.overview: Year 2 probability used single events. Year 3 handles compound events: the probability that A and B both occur, that A or B occurs, and the probability of A given that B has already occurred (conditional probability). It also covers independent trials repeated several times and draws without replacement. The unifying rule is the multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A).
introduction.placementRelevance: Compound and conditional probability questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds with cards, dice, coins and balls in bags.
introduction.realWorldContext: Quality control sampling, medical test accuracy and risk assessment depend on conditional probability.

learningObjectives: Use the multiplication rule with and without independence
Solve repeated-trial problems (at least one, exactly k)
Handle draws with and without replacement
Use the complement for "at least" events

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). For independent events P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).

coreDefinitions: Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B).
Independent events: P(A | B) = P(A); equivalently P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together: P(A and B) = 0.
Binomial trials: probability of exactly k successes in n independent trials = nCk pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ.
Without replacement: the sample space shrinks after each draw.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Conditional probability restricts the sample space to the cases where the given event has occurred. The probability of A given B is the share of B's cases in which A also happens.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Define the events, decide independence, write the multiplication rule, and compute. For "at least one", compute 1 − P(none).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Multiplication rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A)

mainNarrative: For sequential draws without replacement multiply the changing probabilities. From a bag with 5 red and 3 green balls, P(both red) = (5/8)(4/7) = 5/14.

Conditional probability restricts the sample space. Two dice are thrown. Given that the first shows 3, the sum is 8 only if the second shows 5, so P = 1/6. Given that the sum is 8 (5 outcomes), the probability that the first die is 3 is 1/5.
For repeated independent trials, use the binomial formula. P(exactly 2 heads in 3 tosses) = 3C2 (1/2)³ = 3/8. For at least one head: 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8.
With replacement, trials are independent and the probabilities stay the same. Drawing two cards with replacement, P(both aces) = (4/52)² = 1/169. Without replacement it is (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221.
The addition rule with overlap: P(king or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13.

deepDiveAspects.title: Independent vs exclusive
deepDiveAspects.content: Exclusive events have P(A and B) = 0, so they are dependent (if A occurs, B cannot). Independent events overlap in proportion to their probabilities.

deepDiveAspects.title: Order does not matter in the total
deepDiveAspects.content: P(red then green) and P(green then red) are equal when drawing without replacement; use combinations for "one of each".

solvedExamples.title: Without replacement
solvedExamples.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 green balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second draw has one fewer red and one fewer ball.

solvedExamples.title: Conditional probability
solvedExamples.question: Two dice are thrown. Find the probability that the sum is 8 given that the first die shows 3.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Only outcomes with the first die 3 are relevant.

solvedExamples.title: At least one
solvedExamples.question: A fair coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability of getting at least one head.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Multiply sequential fractions; restrict the sample space for conditions; use 1 − P(none) for at least one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing P(A | B) and P(B | A)
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The given event is the denominator.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Probabilities must lie in [0, 1]; for sequential draws the answer is less than each factor.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the events in words first.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Conditional probability leads to Bayes' theorem.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find a draw probability without replacement?
Can I use the binomial formula?
